body:
> How does sse4.2 (x86_64 SIMD) map to WebAssembly?

Emscripten provides a [translation layer](https://emscripten.org/docs/porting/simd.html#compiling-simd-code-targeting-x86-sse-instruction-sets) between the two, and Jolt relies on this translation layer, as it doesn't have any direct WASM SIMD implementation at the moment. Jolt does however add `-msse4.2` as part of its CMake build to make use of this, as seen [here](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/d497df2b9b0fa9aaf41295e1406079c23148232d/Jolt/Jolt.cmake#L639-L642).

From what I understand, this is entirely detached from any sort of hardware requirement, as the WASM runtime is free to do emulation on their end as well. For example, V8 seems to set its [hardware limit](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/2b7982ddc599b3554de17bc402aba9aad2b346d1/src/codegen/x64/assembler-x64.cc#L79-L85) at SSE4.1, with [some emulation](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/19160f94a76de07b3f849f73b5d6ee2c893b5aff/src/wasm/baseline/x64/liftoff-assembler-x64-inl.h#L2999-L3006) for the one SSE4.2 instruction that's mappable to WASM SIMD (`_mm_cmpgt_epi64`).

What's not super clear to me is what happens if you provide `-msimd128` but don't provide `-msse4.2` to Emscripten? Will Emscripten still only implicitly emit WASM SIMD instructions for what would be SSE2 equivalent instructions, like it would if you were compiling for x86-64, or will it assume some saner default (like SSE4.1)? The explicit intrinsics that Jolt uses should presumably be safe to execute regardless, unlike on native platforms.

It would seem to me to be entirely safe to just define `-msse4.2` globally across the entire codebase and maybe then also get some wins from other third-party libraries that are not looking for `__wasm_simd128__`. It might be a good idea to define `WASM_SIMD_COMPAT_SLOW` though, as mentioned in that Emscripten documentation, to prevent hitting any of the slowly emulated ones.
